relations.myth: Perkūnas pursues the hiding devil during thunderstorms
relations.note: Perkūnas attacks Velnias with lightning as he hides in natural objects, animals, or people.
Later interpretations infer that Perkūnas is Dievas’s son from Dievaitis and Christianized folklore.
Latvian songs place Dievs and Pērkons together in a divine dance.
Christianized folklore makes Pērkons an agent who carries out the high God’s punishments.
Modern synthetic accounts pair Perkūnas with the earth goddess Žemyna; no early source confirms the marriage.
Regional folklore sometimes links Perkūnas matrimonially with Laumė or a female atmospheric being.
After Pērkons strikes the celestial tree, Saulė mourns or gathers its golden branches.

relations.myth: Pērkons disrupts the Sun daughter’s wedding
relations.note: Celestial-wedding variants make Pērkons oppose or disrupt the wedding party involving Saules meita.

relations.myth: Perkūnas strikes the celestial wedding tree
relations.note: Perkūnas strikes a tree in a celestial-wedding song associated with Aušrinė.
Some variants attach Māra’s handling or advice about bloody garments to the heavenly-tree episode.

relations.myth: Three gods appear at the sacred oak
relations.note: Grunau places Perkuno and Potrimpo together in an embellished Prussian divine triad.

relations.myth: Three gods appear at the sacred oak
relations.note: Grunau places Perkuno and Patollo together in an embellished Prussian divine triad.

relations.myth: Gods worshipped by Mindaugas and Lithuanians
relations.note: Andajus and Perkūnas appear in the same Lithuanian divine list without narrative interaction.

relations.myth: Gods worshipped by Mindaugas and Lithuanians
relations.note: Žvorūna and Perkūnas appear in the same Lithuanian divine list without narrative interaction.

relations.myth: Gods worshipped by Mindaugas and Lithuanians
relations.note: Teliavelis and Perkūnas appear in the same Lithuanian divine list without narrative interaction.
Early-modern Christian writers identify or translate Perkūnas as the Roman thunder god Jupiter.
